blocks.text: Supervised fine-tuning, SFT, is the process of training a pretrained model on a dataset of labeled input, output pairs, adjusting its weights so it learns to reliably produce the correct output for each kind of input it is shown.

It is the most direct, most widely applied form of fine-tuning covered in this course, and nearly every topic in the surrounding modules, dataset preparation, LoRA, training infrastructure, ultimately supports running an SFT process well.
1. Supervised Fine-Tuning, A Precise Definition
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471813862-766288302.png

The word supervised describes exactly what happens, every training example carries a known correct answer, and the training process adjusts the model to make its predictions match that known answer more closely over time.

This is directly opposite to unsupervised approaches like continued pretraining, covered in the earlier Types of Fine-Tuning topic, which use unlabeled data and a broader objective rather than explicit correct answers per example.
2. The Supervised Part, Labeled Input Output Pairs

blocks.alt: The Supervised Part, Labeled Input Output Pairs
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471813862-595016907.png

Every SFT training example consists of an input, whatever the model is given, and the correct output, exactly what the model should learn to produce for that input, the same basic shape covered throughout the Dataset Preparation for LLMs module.
3. How SFT Fits Into the Larger Fine-Tuning Landscape

blocks.alt: How SFT Fits Into the Larger Fine-Tuning Landscape
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471813863-797201224.png

SFT is not a single specific method, it is the general training approach, full fine-tuning and parameter efficient fine-tuning are both ways of running SFT, and instruction tuning, covered in the next topic, is a common style of SFT applied specifically to instruction following behavior.

blocks.text: 4. The SFT Training Objective
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471813863-253143797.png

At each training step, the model produces a prediction for a given input, that prediction is compared against the correct target output through a loss function, covered in full depth in the dedicated Loss Functions module later in this course, and the resulting loss value drives a small update to the model weights.

code.content:
# A simplified SFT training step
prediction = model(example.input_tokens)
loss = compute_loss(prediction, example.target_tokens)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

blocks.text: 5. What a Typical SFT Dataset Looks Like

blocks.alt: What a Typical SFT Dataset Looks Like
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471813863-25524561.png

An SFT dataset can be narrow, focused on one specific task, or broad, covering many different task types at once, an important distinction covered directly in the later Task-Specific Fine-Tuning and Multi-Task Fine-Tuning topics of this same module.
6. SFT vs Continued Pretraining, Revisited
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471813864-989999739.png

While SFT often still uses next token prediction under the hood, the crucial difference from pretraining is that every SFT example has one specific, known correct target, the model is being pushed toward a particular right answer, not just toward producing plausible text in general.

blocks.title: This distinction matters for understanding loss
blocks.content: Because SFT targets a specific correct output per example, its loss calculation and label masking, covered in the Tokenization Pipeline topic, are structured very differently from the broad, unlabeled objective used in pretraining.

blocks.text: 7. SFT as the Foundation Before Alignment Training

blocks.alt: SFT as the Foundation Before Alignment Training
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471813864-406360934.png

For most modern conversational assistants, SFT is the first training stage applied after pretraining, teaching the model to follow instructions and produce useful responses, with alignment training, covered in its own dedicated module later in this course, typically applied afterward to further shape behavior around human preferences.
8. A Minimal SFT Example End to End

Picture a single SFT example, the input is a customer question, and the target output is the ideal support reply. Across thousands of such examples, SFT gradually shifts the model default behavior toward producing replies that resemble those correct examples, exactly the mechanism underlying most of the practical fine-tuning use cases discussed throughout this course.
9. When SFT Alone Is Enough

For many practical applications, a well built SFT dataset and a properly run SFT training pass are sufficient on their own, without needing the additional alignment training stage, particularly for narrow, well defined tasks where safety and open ended preference alignment are less of a concern.
Worked Example

A team wants a model that reliably converts freeform meeting notes into a structured summary with action items. They build an SFT dataset of two thousand note, summary pairs and run a standard SFT training pass, using the dataset preparation techniques from the previous module.

The resulting model reliably produces structured summaries, since SFT directly taught it, through many labeled examples, exactly what a correct output looks like for this specific task, without needing any further alignment stage for this narrow, well defined use case.
Common Mistakes

items: Confusing SFT, the general approach, with a specific method like full fine-tuning or LoRA, which are ways of running SFT
Assuming SFT alone always requires a subsequent alignment training stage, when many narrow tasks do not need it
Treating SFT and continued pretraining as interchangeable, when they use fundamentally different kinds of data and objectives
Underestimating how directly SFT quality depends on the quality of the labeled dataset preparation covered in earlier modules

blocks.text: Practice

For a task you have in mind, sketch what a single labeled SFT example would look like, the exact input and the exact correct target output, and consider whether SFT alone would likely be sufficient for that task or whether a further alignment stage would matter.
Key Takeaway

Supervised fine-tuning trains a pretrained model on labeled input, output pairs so it learns to reliably produce a specific correct target for each kind of input, and it serves as the general umbrella approach underlying full fine-tuning, parameter efficient methods, and instruction tuning alike, forming the foundation most fine-tuning projects in this course build on.
